This report provides an overview of the state and federal funds dedicated to Hurricane Helene relief and recovery efforts through June 30, 2025, and how North Carolina is using those resources to aid affected communities as required by SL 2025-2 (HB 47) § 4.1(g-h) .Unless otherwise noted, this third quarterly report encompasses activities from the onset of the storm through June 30, 2025.
Hurricane Helene reached North Carolina on Friday, September 27, 2024, generating historic rainfall, strong winds, landslides, and tornadoes, among other weather impacts.
President Biden subsequently declared a Major Disaster, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) designated 39 counties for federal disaster assistance.
An estimated 4.6 million people – more than 40% of the state’s population – live in one of the designated counties.
The region accounts for 45% of the state’s GDP.
Hurricane Helene had a significant, long-term impact on western North Carolina.
In addition to the devastating loss of more than 100 lives, the storm destroyed thousands of homes and damaged tens of thousands more.
Millions of North Carolinians lost access to critical services such as water and sewer, electricity, telecommunications, and health care.
Thousands of miles of roads and bridges were damaged, cutting off communities and 1limiting access for residents, first responders, and recovery teams.
The region’s economy has suffered a severe blow, threatening livelihoods and the long-term outlook of some communities.

Estimates as of December 13, 2024, indicated that Helene caused direct damages of $44.4 billion in the region, caused an additional $9.4 billion in indirect or induced damages, and necessitated $5.8 billion more for strengthening and mitigation. 1 Totaling more than $59.6 billion across the state, these damages and needs are more than three times the $16.7 billion impact of Hurricane Florence in 2018.

As of June 30, 2025, the federal government and North Carolina state government had directed approximately $7.6 billion – about 12.8% of the estimated impact of the storm – to aid western North Carolina communities in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene.

The state has provided just over $2.9 billion in funding, including roughly $2 billion in new appropriations and $508 million in reallocations of previously appropriated funds by the North Carolina General Assembly, and at least $413.8 million in existing state operational resources redirected by state agencies toward response and recovery efforts.

In addition, federal funding totaling $1.61 billion has been disbursed, including $1.1 billion in eligibility-based FEMA funding to individuals, businesses, local government, state agencies, and nonprofits.
Another $3.1 billion in federal funding has been awarded to the State of North Carolina but requires additional approval steps before being disbursed to the state.
# $2 billion in state funds had been appropriated as of June 30, 2025.
State agencies are working to deploy funding effectively and efficiently to speed recovery efforts.

The total $2 billion in appropriated state funds includes $331 million for state matching funds to draw down dollars from federal programs and $272 million for loans to local governments or businesses.
Other state appropriations require certain conditions to be met before expenditure.
For example, $120 million was appropriated for the State Home Reconstruction and Repair Program, which the state may begin spending upon completing federally reimbursable contractor procurements.
The remainder of the funds may be spent by state agencies without significant constraints.
In addition to using the funds provided to them by the NCGA specifically for Helene-related purposes, state agencies have also redirected $413 million of the funds they received prior to the storm.
Some portion of expenses for these activities will be eligible for FEMA reimbursement.
But a significant portion will be borne as state opportunity costs – the eƯect of redirecting resources away from other activities.
North Carolina has received a total of $1.6 billion in federal funding as of June 30, 2025.
Of these funds, $1.1 billion of eligibility-based funding has been disbursed or obligated by the Department of Homeland Security Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

Another $540 million has been disbursed by other federal agencies, including from the U.S. Small Business Administration for home and business loans, the U.S. Department of Labor for unemployment insurance, and the Federal Highway Administration for road repairs.
Another $3.1 billion in federal funding has been awarded to the State of North Carolina but requires additional approval steps before being disbursed to the state.

 $1.4 billion will be administered by the Department of Commerce Division of Community Revitalization (DCR) from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) for the state’s single family home repair and reconstruction program.
Applications are open, and construction on homes should begin later this summer.
 The City of Asheville received $225 million in Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR), and its plan has been approved by HUD.

The plan allocates $125 million for Infrastructure; $52 million for Economic Revitalization; $31 million for Housing; approximately $11.2 million for Administration; approximately $3.7 million for Planning; and $2 million for Public Services.

 NC Department of Transportation (DOT) is preparing an authorization request for the US Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) for approximately $1.15 billion, in addition to the $750 million authorization already received.
FHWA’s Emergency Relief Program provides federal funding to repair federal-aid highways and federal lands roads damaged by natural disasters and catastrophic events.
DOT believes there will still be a shortfall of approximately $1 billion for Helene repairs that will need to be filled with state and federal funding.
 NC Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) is administering $685 million from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to repair wastewater treatment and drinking water facilities.
In December 2024, Congress appropriated funds for Helene recovery to the state through HR 10545, The American Relief Act of 2025 (ARA).
In February 2025 the state estimated its 56 expected allocation from the ARA to be approximately $5.95 billion.
As of June 30, 2025, the state is still waiting for federal agencies to disburse $4.2 billion of these appropriated funds to NC agencies.
Federal funding disbursement delays have impacted state agency timelines for several major recovery components.
For example, the timeline for private property debris removal and demolitions has lengthened because of slow and inconsistent disbursements from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

In addition, as of June 30, 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (USDHHS) had not opened the application period for the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) which provides one-time disaster grant funds to child care providers, centers, homes, and Pre-K sites.
Congress appropriated $250 million for the CCDBG in HR 10545, The American Relief Act of 2025 .

North Carolina requested Congress appropriate an additional $11.6 billion in federal funding to address unmet recovery needs, including critical investments in child care infrastructure, child welfare programs, landslide hazard mapping, flood reduction, and water infrastructure projects.
Although the state has invested $2.9 billion of its own funds, this amount combined with federal assistance received thus far still pales in comparison to the estimated total damage of $59.6 billion.
Western North Carolina communities require additional federal assistance to achieve a comprehensive recovery.

Some eligibility-based federal funding streams are winding down.
For example, applications closed for FEMA Individual Assistance and U.S. Small Business Administration loans.
Grants will likely continue to be disbursed over the next several months as applications work their way through the standard processes, but outlays have slowed.
Funding for disaster unemployment assistance also ended.
FEMA programs include Individual Assistance (IA), Public Assistance (PA), and the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), among others.

While IA, PA, and HMGP are eligibility-based and do not require stand-up of new programs, they do require the state to invest alongside the federal government by matching a portion of the funding received.
Of the 100 counties in the state, 39 are eligible for FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) and 26 are eligible for all categories of FEMA public assistance (FEMA Public Assistance Categories A-G).
The state expects to receive about $1.4 billion from the FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) to reduce the long-term risks to people and property from future disasters.

The program provides grants to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments to implement cost-effective measures that seek to minimize disaster damage, enhance community resilience, and reduce reliance on federal disaster assistance.
Eligible projects include infrastructure improvements, property acquisition, flood risk reduction, and community planning.
So far, the state has received an initial $16.3 million for its management costs.
The state is working with counties to batch and submit applications to FEMA on a rolling basis.
